title: Financial Literacy · Episode 1
chapters: Building an emergency fund from scratch

units.t: Financial Literacy. Episode one.
In this episode: Budgeting that actually works, Building an emergency fund from scratch, How compound interest works and How credit scores work.
Part one. Budgeting that actually works.
A budget isn't a diet for your money.
It's a plan that gives every dollar a job, and it takes about 20 minutes to set up.
Plan, then track.
A budget is simply a plan: deciding in advance where your money goes instead of wondering afterwards where it went.
It's not about never spending on fun; it's about spending on what matters to you.
Surveys consistently find money is one of the biggest sources of stress for Australians, and knowing your numbers replaces vague anxiety with a plan.
Start with reality.
Most banking apps sort your spending into categories automatically.
Look back over one to three months.
Many people are surprised by the total of small regular purchases: coffees, takeaway, delivery fees and forgotten subscriptions.
Don't judge yet; just get the facts.
Include irregular costs like car rego, insurance and Christmas by dividing the yearly cost by 12.
The 50/30/20 rule.
A simple starting framework, popularised by US senator and former Harvard professor Elizabeth Warren, is the 50/30/20 rule.
About 50 per cent of after-tax income goes on needs: rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, transport and insurance.
About 30 per cent goes on wants: eating out, entertainment, hobbies and holidays.
And 20 per cent goes on savings and paying down debt faster.
In high-cost cities, needs often take more than half, so treat the numbers as a guide and adjust them to fit your life.
Pay yourself first.
The most effective budgeting habit is automation.
Set up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account on payday, before you can spend it.
Money you never see in your everyday account is much easier not to spend.
Many Australians use 'buckets': separate accounts for bills, everyday spending, savings goals and emergencies.
Life guarantees surprises: a car repair, a vet bill, a job loss.
An emergency fund turns crises into inconveniences.
A common target is three to six months of essential expenses in an easy-access, high-interest savings account.
That sounds like a lot, so start with a smaller goal like $1,000.
Without a buffer, surprises tend to land on a credit card, where they grow.
Clear high-interest debt.
Credit cards often charge around 20 per cent interest, so paying one off is like earning a guaranteed 20 per cent return.
Two popular methods: with the avalanche, you pay the minimum on everything and throw extra money at the debt with the highest interest rate, which saves the most money.
With the snowball, you clear the smallest balance first, building momentum through quick wins.
Be wary of buy now, pay later services too.
They're convenient, but missed payments bring fees and they make it easy to overspend.
Cut leaks, make it stick.
The easiest savings are often recurring costs you've stopped noticing.
Cancel subscriptions you don't use.
Once a year, compare your energy, insurance, internet and phone plans; loyalty is rarely rewarded, and switching can save hundreds of dollars.
The Australian Government's Energy Made Easy site compares electricity and gas offers for free, in Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare.
The best budget is one you'll keep.
Include guilt-free fun money, or you'll eventually rebel.
Check in monthly for 15 minutes.
Give your savings a purpose, like a holiday or house deposit, and expect imperfect months.
This is general information, not personal financial advice; the National Debt Helpline, 1800 007 007, offers free help if debts feel overwhelming.
The key idea: A budget is a plan for your money, and the first step is tracking where it currently goes.
Part two. Building an emergency fund from scratch.
A blown tyre, a vet bill, a sudden gap between jobs: life sends invoices without warning.
An emergency fund turns those moments from a crisis into an inconvenience, and you can start with very little.
A buffer changes everything.
Two people face the same expensive car repair.
One pays from savings, feels annoyed and moves on.
The other uses a credit card, pays interest for months, and when the next surprise hits, the debt grows.
The difference is not income or intelligence; it is a buffer.
A common target is about three months of essential expenses: rent or mortgage, bills, groceries, transport and minimum debt repayments.
Casual workers, freelancers and single-income households may want more.
Starting from zero, break it down: first enough for one surprise bill, then one month of essentials, then two, then three.
Add up essentials from bank statements or use Moneysmart's budget planner.
This is general information, not financial advice.
Where to keep it.
An emergency fund needs to be accessible quickly, but not so close that you dip into it for takeaway.
A separate high-interest savings account, ideally not linked to a card, is a common choice.
Many pay bonus interest only if you meet conditions, such as a monthly deposit and no withdrawals, so read the terms.
Losing the bonus in a month you use the fund is fine.
If you have a home loan with an offset account, money held there reduces your interest.
Deposits in authorised banks, building societies and credit unions are protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme up to a limit; check the current limit at fcs.
gov.
au.
Finding the money.
The most reliable way to save is to make it automatic.
Set up a regular transfer to your emergency account on payday, before you can spend the money.
Start with an amount that doesn't hurt, even a small sum each pay, and raise it when you can.
Add windfalls such as a tax refund, a bonus or money from selling things you no longer use.
When you cut a cost, like cancelling an unused subscription or switching to a cheaper phone plan, redirect that saving straight into the fund so it doesn't disappear into everyday spending.
Some banks offer round-up features that move small change from each purchase into savings, which can help build the habit.
Rules and refills.
An emergency fund only works if it survives until an emergency.
Decide in advance what counts: unexpected, necessary and urgent things, like a failed hot water system, an urgent dental bill, a car repair you need for work, or essentials after losing your job.
Holidays, gifts and planned bills like car registration or insurance are not emergencies.
Predictable costs belong in a separate sinking fund.
Frequent raids may mean your budget needs adjusting, not that you lack willpower.
Using the fund is not failure; it did its job and you avoided debt.
Then restart your automatic transfers and set a realistic timeframe to refill it.
Review your target yearly, as your essential costs change.
If you have nothing yet.
Sometimes the emergency arrives before the fund does.
Avoid the most expensive options first, such as payday loans and some consumer leases.
Ask the business you owe about a payment plan; many tradespeople, vets, utilities and hospitals offer them.

If you receive certain Centrelink payments, Services Australia may give you an advance payment, which you repay from future payments, and there are crisis payments for specific severe situations; check eligibility at servicesaustralia.
gov.
au.
The No Interest Loan Scheme can help eligible people with essential costs.
The National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, offers free financial counselling.
Once the problem is handled, start your fund, even with a tiny first deposit.
The key idea: An emergency fund stops surprise costs becoming high-interest debt, and about three months of essentials is a common target.
Part three. How compound interest works.
Interest that earns interest.
It's the most powerful force in personal finance, working for you or against you.
Interest on interest.
Interest is the price of money: what a bank pays you for your savings, or a lender charges you for borrowing.
Simple interest is paid only on your original amount, the principal.
Compound interest is paid on the principal plus the interest you've already earned.
Your money earns money, and then that money earns money too.
The same maths applies to investments that reinvest their returns.
Put $10,000 in an account paying 5 per cent a year and leave the interest in.
After one year you have $10,500.
In year two you earn 5 per cent on $10,500, so you gain $525 and have $11,025.
The extra $25 is interest on interest.
After 10 years you'd have about $16,300; after 20, about $26,500; after 30, about $43,200, more than four times the original, without adding a dollar.
Time beats amount.
Growth curves upward, gently at first, then steeply.
In the example above, the first 10 years added about $6,300, while the last 10 added about $16,700 from the same $10,000.
Many people give up in the early years, just before the curve bends upwards.
Here's a famous comparison at a 7 per cent annual return.
Alex invests $5,000 a year from age 25 to 35, then stops: $50,000 in total.
Sam starts at 35 and invests $5,000 every year until 65: $150,000 in total.
At 65, Alex has more than Sam despite contributing a third as much, because Alex's money had an extra decade to compound.
It's never too late to start, but small amounts started early are extraordinarily powerful.
The rule of 72.
A handy shortcut: divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.
At 6 per cent, it doubles in about 12 years.
At 9 per cent, about 8 years.
At 2 per cent, a typical savings rate in some years, about 36 years.
It works in reverse too: to double your money in 10 years, you'd need a return of about 7.
2 per cent.
The rule is an approximation, but it's accurate enough for rates between about 2 per cent and 15 per cent.
It works against you.
Compounding is just as powerful in reverse.
Credit cards in Australia often charge around 20 per cent interest a year.
By the rule of 72, an unpaid balance would roughly double in under four years.
Paying only the minimum each month can stretch a modest debt over a decade or more, costing far more in interest than the original purchase.
That's why paying down high-interest debt is often one of the best 'returns' you can get: it's a guaranteed saving at that rate.
Frequency, fees, inflation.
Interest can be added annually, monthly or even daily.
The more often it's added, the sooner it earns interest itself.
At 5 per cent, monthly compounding gives an effective annual return of about 5.
12 per cent, against 5 per cent for yearly compounding.
When comparing savings accounts, look for the effective annual rate, and watch for 'bonus' rates that only apply if you meet conditions each month.
Anything expressed as a yearly percentage compounds, including costs.
A super or investment fund charging 1 per cent more in fees each year doesn't sound like much, but over 30 years it can cut your final balance by tens of thousands of dollars.
Inflation compounds too, shrinking what your money can buy.
So start early, be patient, keep fees low and pay off expensive debt.
The key idea: Compound interest pays interest on your original money plus the interest already earned, so growth snowballs.
Part four. How credit scores work.
A three- or four-digit number can decide whether you get a loan, and at what rate.
Here's how to see yours for free.
What a score is.
When you apply for a loan, credit card, phone plan or sometimes even a utility account, the provider checks your credit history to judge how likely you are to repay.
A credit score boils that history into a single number.
A higher score suggests lower risk, which can mean easier approval and sometimes better interest rates.
A low score doesn't mean rejection everywhere, but it can limit your options.
In Australia, credit reports are kept by credit reporting bodies, mainly Equifax, Experian and illion.
Each calculates its own score on its own scale: Equifax uses 0 to 1,200, while Experian and illion use 0 to 1,000.
So your score can differ between them.
What's in your report.
Your credit report includes personal details, the credit accounts you hold and their limits, and every time you've applied for credit, called an enquiry.
It also includes up to 24 months of repayment history, showing whether you paid on time each month.
Defaults, which are overdue debts of $150 or more that a lender has reported, can also appear, along with bankruptcies and similar insolvency records.
These generally stay on your report for years.
Lenders may check one or more of the credit reporting bodies when you apply, and each may hold slightly different information.
What helps and hurts.
The single biggest factor is paying bills and loan repayments on time, every time.
Setting up direct debits for at least the minimum payment helps avoid accidental misses.
Keep credit card limits no higher than you need, since lenders consider your total available credit, not just what you've used.
A long, steady history of well-managed accounts also works in your favour.
Missing repayments, especially by more than 14 days, can show up in your history.
Defaults are more serious and can stay on your report for five years even after you pay them.
Many credit applications in a short period can lower your score, because it can look like financial stress.
Buy now, pay later became regulated as credit in 2025, so providers may now check and report to credit bureaus.
Check and correct.
You have the right to a free credit report from each credit reporting body every three months, and also if you've been refused credit recently.
Request it directly from Equifax, Experian and illion, and look for the free option, as some services try to sell paid subscriptions.
Checking your own report doesn't hurt your score.
Do it once a year, and before applying for a big loan like a mortgage.
Reports sometimes contain mistakes, such as a debt that isn't yours or a default already paid.
Ask the bureau or the lender to correct it, free of charge.
If it isn't resolved, complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, AFCA.
Be wary of 'credit repair' companies that charge large fees; legitimate negative information can't simply be removed.
Protect your identity.
Identity thieves sometimes use stolen details to apply for credit in your name, which damages your report.
Warning signs include enquiries you didn't make or accounts you don't recognise, which is another reason to check your report regularly.
If you think your identity has been stolen, you can ask the credit reporting bodies to place a ban on your credit file, stopping anyone accessing it for 21 days, extendable.
IDCARE, a free national service, can help you respond.
Guard your licence, passport and Medicare details carefully.
The key idea: A credit score boils your credit history into one number that lenders use to judge how likely you are to repay.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the first step in building a budget?
Answer. Tracking where your money currently goes.
Question two. What is the main job of an emergency fund?
Answer. To keep surprise costs from becoming debt.
Question three. What makes compound interest different from simple interest?
Answer. You earn interest on earlier interest too.
Question four. What is a credit score for?
Answer. It sums up your history for lenders.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
